texts.body:
Promo (part 1)
Welcome to LOGUS for beginners the first part of the bestselling English course on Udemy.
LOGUS is a very intensive spoken English course in the form of a cartoon designed for people who are tired of learning the language from those boring textbooks, and listening to nerdy teachers.
It was created for people who want to finally learn to think in English, and to speak it fluently just like their native language.
You think it’s impossible?
We’ll prove you wrong.
This course begins with the most basic things you need to start speaking, and it gradually goes into the intermediate level towards the end of the course.
And the best part is you start speaking instantly.
Right from the first lesson.
Isn’t that cool?
And make no mistake here this is not your supplementary short course this is a full-blown course that guides you from the very basics of the English language to the Intermediate level step by step.
100% of the lesson is speaking in a form of a dialogue.
You listen answer and ask questions, and immediately see if you’ve made a mistake.
And if you did nothing to worry about, because you will repeat every grammar construction, so many times later on that they will all be recorded directly in your brain without drowning you in the grammar rules.
Where it’s necessary you’ll be given very clear and simple explanations of essential grammar.
And at the end of each chapter you will take a milestone test to check your progress.
You will learn over 1000 of the most important English words and phrases.
And by learning I don’t mean memorizing.
I mean learning in such a way that you can use them effortlessly in your speech without thinking.
Each lesson you’ll be hearing and saying over 1200 words.
That amount of language practice is enough to make you a fluent speaker in no time.
And just imagine how many more job opportunities you will have with fluent English like this, and this course is a must-have component for you if you’re planning to take IELTS or TOEFL tests in the future.
So, if you want to stop speaking English like a potato when traveling studying or when talking to your business partners this is the right course for you.
Buy it now for this special promo price before it goes ALL the way up!
And with the 30-day return policy, this is a safe bet.
Click that buy button right now, and learn to speak English once and for all.

texts.body:
Instruction (part 2)
Welcome to the tutorial video.
Watch it till the very end in order to avoid confusion about what you should do, and how this course works.
What exactly is going to happen starting from the next video?
You’ll learn the new vocabulary and grammar, then I’ll be asking you lots and lots of questions on different topics.
When you see this message it means you have to start answering the question aloud.
Not in whisper not to yourself.
You have to speak aloud.
Moreover you have to pronounce the full answer to the question.
For example, if I ask you.
Where do you live?
You’ll have to answer.
I live in my apartment.
The answer like uh… in my apartment is not going to cut it.
Always give the full answer.
I’ll give you just enough time to answer the question.
After that you’ll hear the correct answer.
If your answer is different in grammar or in vocabulary stop the video try to analyze your mistake go back a few seconds, and repeat the right answer after me.
If the time I give you to answer isn’t enough it means you have to speed up the pace.
Go through the same lesson one more time until you can fit in the timeframe.
If you stop the video to give yourself more time to answer , it’s cheating.
Don’t do that when you see this message you have to repeat the question I asked you.
So, pay close attention to the questions I ask.
Translations.
You will hear all the dialogues new vocabulary and grammar in English.
But I bet you’ll want to have it all translated.
If you’re using a computer click on the “CC” button below.
If you’re using a mobile app tap on the video while playing it, and at the top you will see the “CC” menu tap on it, and choose the language you want vocabulary and grammar to be translated into, but regardless of the language you choose all the dialogues will appear in English only.
Vocabulary and grammar parts will be translated.
Repetition.
If you want to learn to think in English repetition is extremely important.
That’s why each lesson begins with repetition of what you learned before.
Do not skip the repetition and go straight to the new material.
This way you will never become fluent 1 lesson at a time.
The lessons are pretty long.
So, make sure you have about an hour and a half for your English each day without being disturbed.
For the maximum effect you should take one lesson each day.
But make sure you take not less than 3 lessons per week.
Good luck.
And see you in the lesson 1.

You probably have noticed “a” before each noun.
A chair a phone a table a laptop.
What is “a” and when do we use it?
“A” is an article.
We use it before singular nouns.
It might sound weird to you especially if you don’t have articles in your native language.
But they are very important in English.
So, always put the article “a” before a singular noun.
Don’t worry, you’ll get used to it.

We use “a” before non-particular general objects or people.

We’ve never seen this man before.

For example.
I want to talk about this laptop to say that it is sitting on the table.

In this example we want to talk about a very specific laptop.
This one.

The table.

Now let’s learn to make a plural form of nouns.
One table.

Very easy.
But there are a couple of exceptions.
One man with “A”.
But two MEN with E.

“Two mans” is wrong.
Another exception.
One woman with “A”.
But “two women” with E.
Two women.
Three women.
So, the plural of “man” is “men” with an “E”.
And the plural of “woman” is “women” with an E.
The word “is” has two siblings “am” and “are” Let me explain.
We use “is” with a singular object.
For example.
The man is on the chair.
One man.
The chair is on the floor.
One chair.
But For plural objects we use “are”.
For example.
This car is expensive.
One car this one but these cars are expensive these two cars.
This man is rich “is” because it’s one man “These men are rich” “are", because we have a plural noun “men”.
So, we use “is” with one object or person and “are” with more than one object or person.
And we use “am” only with “I”.
I am a teacher.
I am a doctor.
And so on.
Just like with “is”, in questions “are” and “am” go before the subject we describe.
For example.
We are friends it’s a statement “Are we friends?”
Is a question “I am a teacher” is a statement “Am I a doctor?”
Is a question.
And in negative we add “not” after “are” and after “am”.
For example.
These cars are not cheap.
I am not a teacher.
Also “are not” is often contracted into “aren’t”.
Keep that in mind.
These cars are not cheap is the same as these cars aren’t cheap.
Pronouns.
The most common pronouns in English are I you he she it we and they.
With “I” we use “am”.
I am a teacher.
With “you” we use “are” You are a student.
With “he”, “she” and “it” we use “is”.
He is a student.
She is a student.
It is a table.
With “we” and “they” we use “are”.
We are in the class.
They are in the class.

This might seem weird to you if you have only one present tense one past tense, and one future tense in your language that in English we have several present several past, and several future tenses.
For example one present tense for actions that happen on a regular basis, and one present tense for actions that are happening right now.
All tenses in English have their own grammar rules, and their own indicative words.
Words that indicate the tense.
Those are very important words and you need to pay very close attention to them.
You are already familiar with several indicative words “is” for describing singular objects or people “are” for describing plural objects and “am” when you talk about yourself.
Today we’re going to learn to describe actions.
Actions that happen on a regular basis like.
Every day once a week twice a month etc.
But not at this moment.
The tense is called “simple present”.
For example.
I drink three cups of coffee a day.

Three times a day.

Let me show you how to use this tense correctly.
I sleep for 6 hours every night “I” the subject followed by the base form of the verb “sleep”.

Subject “we”, followed by the base form of the verb “play”.
What is the base form of the verb?
You see verbs in English can change their form depending on the tense and gender.
By base form.
I mean the form of the verb you will find in a dictionary.
Without any endings or suffixes.
They take a bus to work.
Subject “they” followed by the base form of the verb “take”.
They take a bus to work.
This sentence means that they usually take the bus maybe every day, or on working days, but not at this moment.

Do you drink coffee in the morning?

How many cups of coffee do you drink in the morning?
Subject “you” always followed by the action “drink”.
And before the subject…

I don’t drink tea in the morning.
You don’t like coffee with milk.
I don’t have a car.

Now let’s see what happens in simple present tense when the subject is “he”, “she” or "it".
We just add the ending “s” or “es” to the verb.
For example.
I drink 2 cups of coffee in the morning but he drinks 2 cups of coffee in the morning.
You see the ending “s” here?
Good.
We put it here because the subject is “he”.
Jenifer likes her car “Likes” with the ending “s”, because the subject is “Jenifer” it’s a she.
There are a couple of exceptions here.
The verb “have” We don’t just add “s” to it.
There is no such word “haves”.
When the subject is “he”, “she” or "it" “have” turns into “has” French fries have a lot of salt in them but this cake has a lot of sugar in it.
This cake is “it” “It has” "this cake has" in questions our indicative word the one we put before the subject is not “do” but “does”.
Or example:.
Does John drive a car?
Subject “John”, it’s a “he”, ore it we have the indicative word “does”, and after it we have our verb “drive”.
Notice that it doesn’t have the ending “s” anymore.
Another example.
How many cups of coffee does Lisa drink in the morning?
The same story.
Subject "Lisa" before it we have the indicative word “does”, because Lisa is a she and after it we have our verb “drink” without the ending “s”.
In negative we put “does not” or its contraction “doesn’t” after the subject.
For example.
John doesn’t have a car.
Lisa doesn’t like tea.
Sarah doesn’t work hard "Who" in questions.
Let’s look at this example.
John likes Lisa.
And now let’s ask questions with “Who” 2 questions, actually.
In one “who” will be about John, and in another one, about “Lisa”.
So, if we know that John likes somebody, but we don’t know who he likes we ask in the following way:.
Who does John like?
Subject “John”, before it we have our indicative word “does” and after it we have our main verb “like”.
Who does John like?
And what if we know that somebody likes Lisa, but we don’t know who, and we want to ask a question about it we do it this way who likes Lisa?
Something’s strange here.
We don’t have an indicative word “does”.
Why not?
Well, let’s look closer.
We have our main verb here, “likes”, but do we have the subject?
No, we don’t.
It’s unknown.
So, if we don’t have the subject, we don’t put an indicative word before it.
Let’s see another example.
Mason lives with his parents.
And now let’s ask two questions with “who” in one his parents will be unknown in the second one.
Mason will be unknown.
Who does Mason live with?
We have our subject Mason before it we have our indicative word “does” and after it e have our main verb “live” without the ending “s”.
Who lives with his parents?
Here the subject is unknown.
Mason is unknown.
Instead of Mason we have “who” no subject no indicative word “does”.

We use “some” in positive statements and in questions.
For example.

There is another word with a similar meaning “any”, but we use it in questions and negative statements.
For example.

Positive answer:.

Positive response:.

Negative response:.

And there is another word “no”, which is only used in negative sentences.
You can say.
I don’t drink any coffee in the morning or I drink no coffee in the morning.

Again we use "some" in positive sentences and in questions "Any" in questions and in negative sentences and “no” only in negative sentences.

There are several verbs in English that behave in a different way than all other verbs.
In order not to make things too complicated for you let’s just call these words “special”.
One of these special words is “can”, which means “be able to” Let’s look at several examples.
I can speak English.
We can drink three bottles of whiskey in a few hours "what’s so special about this word" you might ask?
Keep looking.
He can stay under water for 4 minutes.
Still not seeing it?
Look here.
We didn’t add “s” here, although the subject is “he”.
She can cook a chocolate cake for the party no “s” here either.
We don’t say.
She CANS cook a chocolate cake for the party.
So, the first special thing about “can” is we don’t add “s” to it.
Another thing questions.
If the statement looks like this He can stay under water for 4 minutes the question will look like this DOES he can stay under water for 4 minutes?
No-no-no-no-no!
I’m just kidding.
It’s not how we ask a question with “can” Look carefully.
Can he stay under water for 4 minutes?
“He can stay” “can he stay?”
How long can he stay under water?
"Can he stay?"
Where can he stay for 4 minutes?
"Can he stay?"
Statement:.
She can cook a chocolate cake for the party.
Question:.
Can she cook a chocolate cake for the party?
"She can" "can she?"
How many chocolate cakes can she cook for the party?
When can she cook a chocolate cake?
One more special thing about “can” negative statements.
In negative statements, we use “cannot” or its contraction “can’t”.
I can’t stay under water for 10 minutes.
She can’t cook 10 cakes in one hour.
